## Descriptive overview

Before the models, we show the observed data they summarise. @fig-accuracy-trajectory
plots the raw learning trajectory, which is also the direct check on the
linear-in-session assumption the models make. @fig-predictor-corr shows the baseline
predictors' intercorrelations and @tbl-predictor-desc gives the same predictors
numerically. The per-measure distributions (@fig-predictor-dist) and the resting-state
spectra behind the band-power and individual-alpha-frequency measures (@fig-rs-psd) are
given in the online supplementary material (@apx-supplementary), which is deposited with
the analysis code in this paper's repository. These displays cover three different
frames, as their notes state. @fig-predictor-dist plots the stored records for each measure one
panel at a time, so the number of points differs between panels. @fig-predictor-corr and
@tbl-predictor-desc cover the participants who have both a baseline cognitive battery and
an eyes-closed resting-state spectrum, and @fig-rs-psd covers every recorded spectrum. All
three are wider than the `r proj_n(projpath_raw)` participants of the fitted raw-band
model, so their counts describe the measures rather than the models.

One feature of the learning trajectory bears on how *rate* and *attainment* should be read,
since both terms would otherwise suggest improvement. Mean accuracy is highest
at each property's first session and lower at its last, in every property and both
mini-languages. The session term is credibly negative both pooled
(`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive"]], "z_session_time")`) and within gender
agreement (`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive_gender"]], "z_session_time")`). In
the pooled model, this partly reflects the design: properties of increasing difficulty
enter cumulatively across sessions, so later sessions sample harder material (see *Learning
outcome and model structure*). Within gender agreement, which is sampled throughout, that
explanation does not apply, and we record the decline as an unexplained feature of these
data. Throughout what follows, *rate* is the slope of this trajectory and *attainment* its
model-implied end point, whichever way the trajectory runs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-accuracy-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Observed Grammaticality-Judgement Accuracy Across Sessions, by Grammatical Property and Mini-Language"
#| apa-note: "Thin lines are individual participants, and the ribbon is a 95% confidence interval computed between participants, the sampling unit being participants and not trials. This is the raw trajectory the joint model summarises, and the direct check on the linear-in-session assumption."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
if (!is.null(acc_traj_tbl)) {
  gc <- acc_traj_tbl[acc_traj_tbl$level == "group_cell" & !is.na(acc_traj_tbl$grammatical_property), ]
  bp <- acc_traj_tbl[acc_traj_tbl$level == "participant_cell" &
                       !is.na(acc_traj_tbl$grammatical_property), ]
  if (!nrow(bp)) bp <- NULL
  # Order the panels by the session in which each property was introduced (gender
  # agreement in Session 2, differential object marking in Session 3, verb-object
  # number agreement in Session 4). The column is character, so without an explicit
  # factor the panels would fall alphabetically and scramble the design. This must
  # precede the ggplot()/geom_line() calls below, which capture their data by value.
  .prop_order <- c("gender_agreement", "differential_object_marking",
                   "verb_object_number_agreement")
  prop_lab <- as_labeller(c(gender_agreement = "Gender agreement",
                            differential_object_marking = "Differential object marking",
                            verb_object_number_agreement = "Verb-object number agreement"))
  gc$grammatical_property <- factor(gc$grammatical_property, levels = .prop_order)
  if (!is.null(bp)) bp$grammatical_property <- factor(bp$grammatical_property,
                                                      levels = .prop_order)
  p <- ggplot(gc, aes(session, mean_accuracy, colour = mini_language))
  if (!is.null(bp)) p <- p + geom_line(data = bp,
                                       aes(session, mean_accuracy,
                                           group = interaction(participant_lab_ID, mini_language)),
                                       colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.5)
  p + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_accuracy - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean_accuracy + 1.96 * se,
                      fill = mini_language), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
    geom_line(aes(linetype = mini_language), linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ grammatical_property, labeller = prop_lab) +
    # Okabe-Ito blue and vermillion, the same pair fig-predictor-forest uses, so every
    # hard-coded scale in the paper draws on the colourblind-safe set the Method names.
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Mini-English` = "#0072B2", `Mini-Norwegian` = "#D55E00"),
                        aesthetics = c("colour", "fill")) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`Mini-English` = "solid", `Mini-Norwegian` = "22")) +
    labs(x = "Session", y = "Proportion correct", colour = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
    les_theme() + theme(legend.position = "top")
} else cat("*Raw accuracy trajectory will appear once `_accuracy_trajectory_descriptives.csv` is present.*")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictor-corr
#| fig-cap: "Pearson Correlations Among the Baseline Predictors"
#| apa-note: "Correlations are computed on the z-scored predictors, over the participants who have both a baseline cognitive battery and an eyes-closed resting-state spectrum, pairwise-complete, so the n behind each cell varies slightly. Only the lower triangle is shown, the redundant mirror and the unit diagonal being omitted. The resting-state band powers are expected to be positively intercorrelated through the shared aperiodic 1/f background, which motivates the specparam robustness check and is why the projpred ranking must be read against this structure."
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 5
if (!is.null(predictor_corr)) {
  ord <- c("digit_span", "stroop_interference", "asrt_learning",
           "delta", "theta", "alpha", "beta", "gamma", "iaf")
  corr_labs <- c(digit_span = "Digit span", stroop_interference = "Stroop",
                 asrt_learning = "ASRT", delta = "Delta", theta = "Theta",
                 alpha = "Alpha", beta = "Beta", gamma = "Gamma", iaf = "IAF")
  strip0 <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
  pc <- predictor_corr
  # Keep one triangle only: drop the redundant upper mirror and the r = 1 diagonal.
  pc <- pc[match(as.character(pc$var1), ord) < match(as.character(pc$var2), ord), ]
  pc$var1 <- factor(pc$var1, levels = ord); pc$var2 <- factor(pc$var2, levels = rev(ord))
  ggplot(pc, aes(var1, var2, fill = r)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = strip0(r)), size = 3) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = les_div[1], mid = les_div[2], high = les_div[3], midpoint = 0,
                         limits = c(-1, 1), labels = function(x) strip0(x, 1)) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = corr_labs) + scale_y_discrete(labels = corr_labs) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
    les_theme() +
    # Blank the specific grid elements, not just the parent: a theme that sets
    # panel.grid.major.x/y explicitly (as depictr's does) is not cleared by setting
    # panel.grid alone, and the grid would then show through the masked triangle.
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          panel.grid = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
} else cat("*Predictor correlation matrix will appear once `_predictor_correlations.csv` is present.*")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictor-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive Statistics for the Baseline Predictors"
#| apa-note: "The frame is the participants who have both a baseline cognitive battery and an eyes-closed resting-state spectrum, which is wider than the sample any Part A model is fitted to, and the n column gives the number contributing to each row. Each row carries its own unit. Because a band power is the spectral density integrated over the band, its unit is squared microvolts and not squared microvolts per hertz."
if (!is.null(predictor_desc) && requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pd <- predictor_desc
  num <- vapply(pd, is.numeric, logical(1)); pd[num] <- lapply(pd[num], round, 2)
  # Map the pipeline's snake_case keys and lowercase headers to reader-facing labels,
  # using the same names the figures use, and carry the unit on each row so the table
  # is readable without the Method. Done defensively: if the artefact's columns ever
  # change, the raw frame is printed rather than the chunk failing.
  .pdl <- c(digit_span = "Working memory: digit span (items correct)",
            stroop_interference = "Inhibitory control: Stroop interference (ms)",
            asrt_learning = "Statistical learning: ASRT difference (ms)",
            delta = "Delta power (µV²)", theta = "Theta power (µV²)",
            alpha = "Alpha power (µV²)", beta = "Beta power (µV²)",
            gamma = "Gamma power (µV², not interpreted)",
            iaf = "Individual alpha frequency (Hz)")
  if (all(c("predictor", "n", "mean", "sd", "median", "min", "max") %in% names(pd))) {
    lab <- unname(.pdl[pd$predictor])
    pd <- data.frame(Predictor = ifelse(is.na(lab), pd$predictor, lab),
                     n = pd$n, M = pd$mean, SD = pd$sd, Mdn = pd$median,
                     Min = pd$min, Max = pd$max, check.names = FALSE)
  }
  knitr::kable(pd)
} else if (is.null(predictor_desc)) cat("*Predictor descriptive table pending `_predictor_descriptives.csv`.*")
```

## Part A: predictors of the learning trajectory

Each predictor enters twice: as a main effect, indexing the overall level of accuracy, and
in interaction with session, indexing the learning *rate*. Because session is standardised,
the main effect is the association at the average session (see Method). Working memory was
the clearest predictor. Higher baseline digit span went with higher overall accuracy,
credibly so for the fully sampled gender-agreement property
(`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive_gender"]], "z_digit_span")`) and positively,
though with an interval that narrowly included zero, in the pooled model
(`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive"]], "z_digit_span")`). Inhibitory control
(`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive"]], "z_stroop")`) and statistical learning
(`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive"]], "z_asrt")`) were not credibly related to
accuracy, in line with their weak-to-null evidence base.

Of the baseline resting-state measures, the band powers were uninformative
(@fig-predictor-forest), but that null must be read against how strongly they are
intercorrelated. Entering the bands simultaneously means each coefficient is the unique
contribution of that band with the others held constant, and the four low-frequency bands
share a great deal of variance (@fig-predictor-corr). Their variance inflation factors are
`r vif_range(c("delta","theta","alpha","beta"))`, which widens their posterior intervals by
roughly `r vif_widen(c("delta","theta","alpha","beta"))` relative to an orthogonal
predictor. Their null coefficients are therefore weakly identified and uninformative about whether those rhythms relate to learning, and they are not directly
comparable to the zero-order band--outcome associations reported in the precedent
literature. Two of the neural predictors escape this: gamma
(VIF `r vif_of("gamma")`) and the individual alpha frequency (VIF `r vif_of("iaf")`) are
close to orthogonal to the rest, so their estimates stand on their own. The one
suggestive signal was the individual alpha frequency, whose association with
gender-agreement accuracy was
`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive_gender"]], "z_iaf")`. The cross-check the
Method promised points the same way without settling it. In the aperiodic
re-parameterisation of the same stratum, fitted to a smaller sample, the
specparam-estimated individual alpha frequency was
`r report_effect("p2_predictive_trajectory_aperiodic_gender", "z_specparam_iaf")`, and the
aperiodic exponent, the quantity the decomposition adds, was
`r report_effect("p2_predictive_trajectory_aperiodic_gender", "z_aperiodic_exponent")`. The learning-*rate*
interactions were uniformly weak (for working memory,
`r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive"]], "z_session_time:z_digit_span")`), consistent with priors that placed their small informative mass on attainment and shrank the rate terms towards zero.

```{r p2-selection}
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(projpath_raw)) {
  cat(sprintf(paste0(
    "To establish which predictors account for the reference model's predictive ",
    "performance, projection-predictive selection was run on %s and on the aperiodic ",
    "re-parameterisation, and it returned the same parsimonious answer throughout.%s ",
    "In the raw-band model, the suggested size was %s: the design scaffold ",
    "(by-participant intercept and session slope, session, grammatical property and their ",
    "interaction) together with working memory (digit span). Digit span was the first ",
    "individual-difference predictor selected, entering at step %s of the forward search, ",
    "exactly the suggested size. Inhibitory control (step %s), statistical learning (step %s) ",
    "and the resting-state band predictors entered only beyond the suggested size, so they ",
    "are not among the terms the search retained. The forward search was capped at projpred's ",
    "default path length, so the lowest-ranked terms, including the individual alpha ",
    "frequency, reported above as a suggestive baseline signal, fell below that cap ",
    "and were not positively ruled out in that stratum.\n\n%s\n\n",
    "The aperiodic re-parameterisation reproduced this ",
    "ordering (suggested size %s), with the aperiodic exponent and offset entering at steps ",
    "%s and %s, well beyond the suggested size, so the $1/f$ background added no predictive ",
    "information the raw bands had missed. That search was capped at the same default path length, ",
    "so the adjusted beta power and the specparam individual alpha frequency were not reached ",
    "in it either, and the same caveat applies to them as to the raw model's tail terms. ",
    "This is a statement about predictive parsimony, not ",
    "evidence that the unselected predictors have no effect [@piironen2020]."),
    projpred_strata(), projpred_gender_caveat(),
    proj_size(projpath_raw), proj_rank(projpath_raw, "z_digit_span"),
    proj_rank(projpath_raw, "z_stroop"), proj_rank(projpath_raw, "z_asrt"),
    projpred_gender_result(),
    proj_size(projpath_aper), proj_rank(projpath_aper, "z_aperiodic_exponent"),
    proj_rank(projpath_aper, "z_aperiodic_offset")))
  if (!is.null(aper_loo_tbl)) {
    both_tie <- isTRUE(aper_loo_tie("pooled")) && isTRUE(aper_loo_tie("gender"))
    verdict <- if (both_tie) {
      "in each case smaller than twice its standard error"
    } else {
      sprintf("%s in the pooled stratum and %s for gender agreement",
              aper_loo("pooled", "verdict"), aper_loo("gender", "verdict"))
    }
    cat(sprintf(paste0(
      "\n\nThe two parameterisations were also compared by PSIS-LOO on the sample they ",
      "share. Because the specparam re-parameterisation is defined for %s of the %s participants, ",
      "the raw-band model was refit on that common subsample so the two are compared on ",
      "identical observations. The aperiodic-minus-raw difference in expected log predictive ",
      "density was %s (SE %s) in the pooled stratum and %s (SE %s) for gender agreement, %s ",
      "[@vehtari2017]. As noted in the Method, this leave-one-trial-out criterion cannot ",
      "detect participant-level predictors, so the near-zero difference is not read as ",
      "evidence that the two characterisations are equivalent.%s"),
      proj_n(projpath_aper), proj_n(projpath_raw),
      aper_loo("pooled", "elpd"), aper_loo("pooled", "se"),
      aper_loo("gender", "elpd"), aper_loo("gender", "se"), verdict,
      aper_kf_sentence()))
  }
  cat("\n")
} else {
  cat("*Projection-predictive selection results appear here once the projpred ",
      "solution-path CSVs are present in `paper_2_plasticity/results/`.*\n", sep = "")
}
```

```{r p2-derived}
#| results: asis
if (results_ready && !is.null(attainment_tbl) && !is.null(reliability_tbl)) {
  af <- function(m) { r <- attainment_tbl[attainment_tbl$model == m, ]
    if (nrow(r) == 1) sprintf("%.2f (95%% CrI [%.2f, %.2f])", r$median, r$ci_low, r$ci_high) else "NA" }
  # Reliabilities are bounded above by 1, so the leading zero is stripped, matching relv()
  # and predrel() elsewhere in the document rather than printing the same quantity two ways.
  rf <- function(m, e) { r <- reliability_tbl[reliability_tbl$model == m & reliability_tbl$effect == e, ]
    if (nrow(r) == 1) sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.2f", r$reliability)) else "NA" }
  cat(sprintf(paste0("Model-implied end-of-training attainment was %s pooled and %s for gender ",
              "agreement. The by-participant level at the average session (the intercept) was ",
              "estimated with high reliability (pooled %s, gender-only %s). The learning-rate slope ",
              "was estimated less reliably (pooled %s, ",
              "gender-only %s), and because the gender-only rate is the least reliably estimated of ",
              "these quantities we do not interpret rate-based individual-difference claims from that ",
              "model.\n"),
      af("p2_predictive_trajectory"), af("p2_predictive_trajectory_gender"),
      rf("p2_predictive_trajectory", "Intercept"), rf("p2_predictive_trajectory_gender", "Intercept"),
      rf("p2_predictive_trajectory", "z_session_time"), rf("p2_predictive_trajectory_gender", "z_session_time")))
}
```

@tbl-reliability gives these outcome reliabilities in full, and
@tbl-predictor-reliability the internal consistency of the three baseline cognitive
indices. Both matter, because the association between a predictor and an outcome is
bounded by the reliability of each. Two of the three cognitive indices are moreover
difference scores, a form whose reliability is typically lower than that of its
components [@draheim2019; @hedge2018].

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictor-forest
#| fig-cap: "Part A Predictor Effects on Overall Accuracy and Learning Rate"
#| apa-note: "Points are posterior medians with 95% equal-tailed credible intervals for each baseline predictor's association with overall accuracy (the main effect, the association at the average session) and with learning rate (the predictor-by-session interaction), in the pooled and gender-agreement-only models. Estimates are on the logit scale: main effects are the change in log-odds of a correct response per SD of the predictor, interaction terms the change in the per-session slope per SD. The two panels share a common x axis so the families are directly comparable, and the rate-interaction terms carry deliberately tighter priors than the main effects. Predictors are ordered working memory, inhibitory control and statistical learning (for the Stroop-based inhibitory-control predictor, higher scores mean poorer inhibition), then the resting-state measures. Intervals excluding zero indicate effects whose direction is well determined."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6
if (results_ready) {
  preds <- c("z_digit_span", "z_stroop", "z_asrt",
             "z_delta", "z_theta", "z_alpha", "z_beta", "z_gamma", "z_iaf")
  rate_terms <- paste0("z_session_time:", preds)
  fp <- post_tbl |>
    filter(model %in% c("p2_predictive_trajectory", "p2_predictive_trajectory_gender"),
           parameter %in% c(preds, rate_terms)) |>
    mutate(Component = ifelse(grepl("^z_session_time:", parameter),
                              "Learning rate (x session)", "Overall accuracy (main effect)"),
           Predictor = factor(.pretty_term(gsub("^z_session_time:", "", parameter)),
                              levels = rev(.pretty_term(preds))),
           Model = ifelse(grepl("_gender$", model), "Gender only", "Pooled"))
  # Both are character, so without explicit levels the facets and the legend fall
  # alphabetically: the rate panel ahead of the main effects, and the gender-only
  # sensitivity model ahead of the primary pooled one, in both cases reversing the order
  # the caption and the surrounding text use.
  fp$Component <- factor(fp$Component,
                         levels = c("Overall accuracy (main effect)", "Learning rate (x session)"))
  fp$Model     <- factor(fp$Model, levels = c("Pooled", "Gender only"))
  if (nrow(fp)) {
    ggplot(fp, aes(x = median, y = Predictor, colour = Model, shape = Model)) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
      geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high),
                      position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
      facet_wrap(~ Component) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = c(Pooled = "#0072B2", `Gender only` = "#D55E00")) +
      scale_shape_manual(values = c(Pooled = 16, `Gender only` = 17)) +
      labs(x = "Posterior estimate (log-odds)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
      les_theme(10) + theme(legend.position = "top")
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reliability
#| tbl-cap: "By-Participant Reliability of the Learning Trajectory"
#| apa-note: "Columns give the group standard deviation, mean posterior standard error, and reliability of the intercept (a participant's level at the average session, since session is standardised) and of the session (rate) slope, for the pooled and gender-agreement-only models. The reliability column is the empirical-Bayes form, the variance of the shrunken by-participant posterior means over the model's between-participant variance. The group SD and mean posterior SE columns are shown for context, not as the terms of a formula."
if (!is.null(reliability_tbl)) {
  # Reliability is bounded above by 1, so its leading zero is stripped, matching relv()
  # and the Results prose. Group SD and the mean posterior SE are unbounded and keep theirs.
  .strip0 <- function(x) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))
  rel <- reliability_tbl |>
    transmute(Model = ifelse(grepl("_gender$", model), "Gender only", "Pooled"),
              Quantity = ifelse(effect == "Intercept", "Overall accuracy (intercept)", "Learning rate (session)"),
              `Group SD` = round(group_sd, 2),
              `Mean posterior SE` = round(mean_posterior_se, 2),
              Reliability = .strip0(reliability))
  knitr::kable(rel)
}
```


## Part B: change in executive function over training

Comparing the first and fifth sessions, working-memory span increased over training,
`r report_effect("p2_cognition_prepost_digit_span", "session_prepost")`. The Stroop
interference effect
(`r report_effect("p2_cognition_prepost_stroop_interference", "session_prepost")`) and the
statistical-learning effect
(`r report_effect("p2_cognition_prepost_asrt_learning", "session_prepost")`) showed no
credible change. In the joint model that lets each index control the others, the pattern
pointed the same way. The joint-model digit-span change was
`r report_effect("p2_cognition_prepost_joint", "session_prepost")`, an interval that,
unlike the single-index model's, includes zero. The estimate is less precise in the
joint specification, which shares one residual standard deviation across the three
measures and adds a by-participant change slope. Relative to that change, the
pre/post shift was smaller for the Stroop interference effect
(`r report_effect("p2_cognition_prepost_joint", "session_prepost:measurestroop_interference")`)
and for the statistical-learning effect
(`r report_effect("p2_cognition_prepost_joint", "session_prepost:measureasrt_learning")`).
These specificity contrasts have credible intervals that include zero (probabilities of
direction `r pd_of("p2_cognition_prepost_joint", "session_prepost:measurestroop_interference")`%
and `r pd_of("p2_cognition_prepost_joint", "session_prepost:measureasrt_learning")`%), so
the evidence that the gain is working-memory-specific is suggestive without being decisive.
@fig-prepost shows these effects.

Two features of the comparison qualify it further. First, the three indices are $z$-scored
within measure and enter the joint model on their recorded polarity, and that polarity is
not aligned across them. A higher digit span is better performance, a higher Stroop
interference score worse (see *Cognitive and neural indices*). A generic practice
improvement would therefore push digit span up and Stroop interference down, in opposite
signed directions, so the digit-span-versus-Stroop contrast is in part an artefact of that
opposition, and it overstates the separation correspondingly. The ASRT comparison is not affected in the same way, since a higher ASRT
score also means better performance and its polarity therefore matches digit span's.
Second, the Stroop index has very low internal consistency here (see *Limitations
and future directions*), which leaves it a noisy control. In task units,
the digit-span change was from `r cog_mean("digit_span", 1)` items correct at Session
1 to `r cog_mean("digit_span", 5)` at Session 5, against
`r cog_mean("stroop_interference", 1)` to `r cog_mean("stroop_interference", 5)` ms of
Stroop interference and `r cog_mean("asrt_learning", 1)` to
`r cog_mean("asrt_learning", 5)` ms of ASRT learning.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prepost
#| fig-cap: "Pre/Post (Session 1 to 5) Change in the Executive-Function Indices"
#| apa-note: "Points are single-index session effects and, for the joint model, the digit-span change and the contrasts of each measure's change against digit span (the reference level). Filled points mark effects whose 95% credible interval excludes zero; open points do not."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
if (results_ready) {
  pp <- post_tbl |>
    filter((model %in% c("p2_cognition_prepost_digit_span",
                         "p2_cognition_prepost_stroop_interference",
                         "p2_cognition_prepost_asrt_learning") & parameter == "session_prepost") |
           (model == "p2_cognition_prepost_joint" &
              parameter %in% c("session_prepost",
                               "session_prepost:measurestroop_interference",
                               "session_prepost:measureasrt_learning"))) |>
    mutate(Effect = dplyr::case_when(
      model == "p2_cognition_prepost_digit_span" ~ "Digit span change",
      model == "p2_cognition_prepost_stroop_interference" ~ "Stroop change",
      model == "p2_cognition_prepost_asrt_learning" ~ "ASRT change",
      parameter == "session_prepost" ~ "Joint: digit-span change",
      parameter == "session_prepost:measurestroop_interference" ~ "Joint: Stroop vs digit span",
      parameter == "session_prepost:measureasrt_learning" ~ "Joint: ASRT vs digit span"),
      Block = ifelse(grepl("^Joint", Effect), "Joint model", "Single-index models"))
  pp$Block  <- factor(pp$Block, levels = c("Single-index models", "Joint model"))
  pp$Effect <- factor(pp$Effect, levels = c(
    "Joint: ASRT vs digit span", "Joint: Stroop vs digit span", "Joint: digit-span change",
    "ASRT change", "Stroop change", "Digit span change"))
  # Filled points mark effects whose 95% interval excludes zero, matching the
  # convention used in the companion paper's ERP forest.
  pp$Credible <- (pp$ci_low > 0) | (pp$ci_high < 0)
  ggplot(pp, aes(x = median, y = Effect)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high, shape = Credible)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 16), guide = "none") +
    facet_grid(Block ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
    labs(x = "Pre/post change (SD units)", y = NULL) +
    les_theme(10)
}
```

# Discussion

This study asked two questions: whether baseline cognitive and neural measures predict
how well adults learn a new grammar (Part A), and whether executive function changes over
the training period (Part B). The answer to the first is selective. Working memory
predicted how well learners did, while inhibitory control,
statistical learning and the resting-state measures added little, and the predictors acted
on the level learners reached, leaving their rate of change unexplained. The answer to the
second falls on the same
capacity: working-memory span was the one index that rose over training.

## Predictors of overall accuracy and learning rate

Working memory was the clearest cognitive predictor of how well learners did, credibly so for gender agreement and in the same direction, though less certainly, when the properties were pooled. This fits the literature placing working memory as the
best-evidenced cognitive correlate of second-language outcomes [@linck2014]. Inhibitory
control and statistical learning, whose evidence base is weak or contested
[@huensch2024; @linckweiss2015; @chen2022; @zhou2024], added little. Because digit span taps storage and not the executive or complex span that carries most of the working-memory--language association [@linck2014], a complex-span measure might well have shown a larger association. If so, the digit-span estimate is unlikely to overstate the working-memory contribution. Digit span is also the weaker of
the phonological short-term memory tasks [@kurokawa2026, on vocabulary outcomes]. That is a conjecture about what another measure would have shown, and it does not bound the estimate reported here.

The baseline resting-state measures
were largely uninformative. Only the individual alpha frequency, a stable, trait-like
measure [@grandy2013trait] related to general cognitive ability
[@klimesch1999; @grandy2013], hinted at a
positive association with overall accuracy, and only in the gender-agreement model, not the
pooled one. It stands as a lead for confirmatory work, and
one to be held lightly. In the same stratum, the projection-predictive search ranked the
individual alpha frequency last, and the estimate is prior-sensitive (see *Priors*). In a
small number of recordings, that measure is also a boundary value with no resolved peak
behind it (see *Cognitive and neural indices*). The null for the band powers contrasts
with reports that resting beta and low-gamma power predict L2 learning *rate* [@prat2016;
@prat2019]. We did estimate the rate analogue. The band-by-session interactions are in the
model and none was credible, though under weakly informative priors their intervals are
wide enough not to exclude effects of the published size. The divergence therefore tracks
our posterior reduction where theirs was right-temporoparietal, together with our
conservative priors and our precision. The two sets of results differ in scope without
contradicting each other. On the gamma half of that comparison, we can say nothing at all.
Our 30--45 Hz band lies above the 30 Hz offline low-pass, so the
measure is not a valid index of gamma-band power and its null is uninformative by
construction (see *Cognitive and neural indices*). Testing the low-gamma part of that result [@prat2016; @prat2019] would need a recording made without a 30 Hz low-pass and with the means to separate myogenic from neuronal activity. The aperiodic re-parameterisation sharpens the neural
null. Had the flat band coefficients merely reflected the
conflation of oscillatory power with the $1/f$ background [@donoghue2020], de-confounding
them should have uncovered signal. That is not what happened. The aperiodic exponent and offset entered the
selection well beyond the suggested size. Under participant-grouped cross-validation,
neither characterisation predicted a held-out learner's trajectory detectably better than
the other.
Against a largely cross-sectional literature relating the aperiodic exponent to cognitive
function, this bounds the question without answering it. At baseline, in this sample, the exponent carried no detectable incremental signal for a longitudinal training outcome, a test cross-sectional designs cannot run. That the two characterisations
could not be distinguished at this sample size also means the band-power nulls above are
not obviously attributable to
periodic/aperiodic conflation, though a comparison this blunt (see the minimum detectable
difference quoted in the Results) cannot establish that they are equivalent.

The predictors
acted on the *level* learners reached, with no detectable purchase on the *rate*. The
predictor-by-session interactions were weak, with the statistical-learning-by-session
term the only one approaching credibility in the raw-band models, and only in the
gender-agreement model. That model's
rate is the least reliably estimated quantity here (reliability
`r relv("p2_predictive_trajectory_gender", "z_session_time")`), so, per the rule stated in the Results, we do not interpret it. In the aperiodic re-parameterisation of that stratum, the adjusted-alpha-by-session term comes at least as close, and we do not interpret it either. The attainment-not-rate asymmetry is not an artefact of the priors' design, a small informative mass on
attainment shrunk towards zero on rate, since it held when the rate terms were re-fit under
weakly informative priors (see *Priors*).

The overall pattern is the one a circumscribed advantage would produce. Had a broad aptitude driven learning, it should have appeared in the statistical-learning index, which is reliably measured and was assessed and modelled identically. In the event, the signal was concentrated in working memory, and the projection-predictive selection retained nothing beyond it. The neural and inhibitory-control comparisons carry much less weight in that argument than the modelling alone suggests: the low-frequency bands are weakly identified, the gamma predictor is not a valid measure, and the Stroop index is too unreliable to have registered an association (see *Limitations and future directions*). The contrast the data can draw is therefore between working memory and statistical learning, the two indices measured well enough to be compared.

The joint model's chief advantage is that it separates attainment from rate. Estimating the by-participant
intercept and slope inside one multilevel model, with their interactions with the predictors,
propagates the uncertainty a two-stage slope analysis would discard [@gelman2005;
@humberg2024]. The by-participant level was estimated with high reliability and the pooled
learning rate less so
(`r relv("p2_predictive_trajectory", "z_session_time")` against `r relv("p2_predictive_trajectory", "Intercept")`),
with the gender-only rate more modest again (`r relv("p2_predictive_trajectory_gender", "z_session_time")`),
so rate-based claims from that model warrant more caution [@hedge2018]. This asymmetry
bears on how aptitude findings indexed by a per-learner slope should be read. If the rate
is in general the less reliably estimated quantity (as it was here even under trial-level
joint modelling, the most favourable case), then slope-indexed predictor effects will be
attenuated and unstable in proportion to that unreliability. Disagreement among them is
then to be expected [@hedge2018; @humberg2024].

## Change in executive function over training

A behavioural change also emerged over training. Working-memory span rose between the first and fifth
sessions, while inhibitory control and statistical learning did not. This comparison lacks a
no-training control group, so on its own a pre/post gain is open to the familiar threats of
an uncontrolled retest: practice effects, regression to the mean, maturation and expectancy
[@shadish2002; @calamia2012; @barnett2005]. Two features of the analysis bound those threats.
First, the gain appeared concentrated in one index. Of three indices measured and retested
identically, only working memory moved. In a joint model across the battery, the pre/post change was larger for digit span than for the co-administered Stroop and statistical-learning measures, in the
same direction and with probabilities of direction of
`r pd_of("p2_cognition_prepost_joint", "session_prepost:measurestroop_interference")`% and
`r pd_of("p2_cognition_prepost_joint", "session_prepost:measureasrt_learning")`%. Those specificity contrasts do
not themselves clear the credibility threshold, since their 95% intervals include zero, and
the joint-model digit-span change does not either, so the concentration remains provisional. The
two co-administered measures nonetheless serve as internal controls. The threats of an
uncontrolled retest act broadly across a battery, so a change concentrated in a single
index is not what they predict. Both controls are imperfect. The Stroop index is of
very low internal consistency here, which leaves it a noisy comparator, and its polarity runs
opposite to digit span's, which inflates that contrast (see *Part B: change in executive
function over training*). Second, that same working-memory measure was the one baseline predictor of
overall accuracy, so the predictive and pre/post analyses converge on it. None of this licenses a
causal claim. Practice effects are not uniform across tasks [@scharfen2018], and even active
control conditions do not fully rule out differential expectancy [@boot2013; @simons2016], so
attributing the gain to the multilingual training specifically would require a matched
no-training group. The result is consistent with a training-related, working-memory-specific change, and no more than that.

## Limitations and future directions

The first limitation is precision. Although the models are fitted to tens of thousands of
trials, the predictor effects are *between*-participant quantities, so their effective sample
size is the number of participants. Only
`r proj_n(projpath_raw)` participants contribute between-participant variance to the
raw-band model and `r proj_n(projpath_aper)` to the aperiodic variant, and eighteen
between-participant coefficients (nine main effects and nine interactions with time) are
estimated from them. That is why even the clearest predictor effect is reported with a wide
interval, and it bounds how strongly any single predictor claim can be made. Effects that do
clear a 95% interval at this sample size are also, on average, overestimates of their true
magnitude, so the working-memory coefficient should be read as evidence of a positive association, not as a calibrated estimate of its size.

A second limitation is that the study is silent on *neural* plasticity. Resting-state EEG was recorded only at
baseline, so the rs-EEG measures bear only on the prediction question. Establishing whether intensive multilingual training reshapes
resting-state activity would need a matched post-training recording, and the behavioural
pre/post comparison reported above cannot stand in for one. A change in working-memory span
is a change in what the task measures, and says nothing about whether the resting rhythms
underlying that capacity have shifted.

A third limitation is the reliability of the predictors themselves, which bounds any
association they can enter into. Because reporting the reliability of the outcome while
leaving the predictors unquantified would be one-sided, we estimated the internal
consistency of each baseline index by permutation split-half with a Spearman--Brown
correction. The result separates two measures that are usually discussed together as
difference scores [@hedge2018]. Statistical learning is estimated highly reliably
(`r predrel("asrt_learning")`) and working-memory span adequately so
(`r predrel("digit_span")`), but Stroop interference is not. Its split-half reliability is
`r predrel("stroop_interference")`, which is close to zero. Almost none of its
between-participant variance is systematic, so the null association between inhibitory control and learning reported here is uninformative, and no
association could have been detected with this measure however large the true effect. That
applies to Part A and to Part B, where the Stroop index is a noisy internal control on the
pre/post comparison. The statistical-learning null carries no such excuse. The ASRT is
estimated highly reliably, so its near-zero coefficient cannot be put down to measurement
error. Even so, failing to
detect an association is not the same as demonstrating its absence. Under a prior centred above zero, the pooled
estimate is `r report_effect(LES_P2_MODELS[["predictive"]], "z_asrt")`. The interval's
upper bound is close to the working-memory median we treat as our clearest effect, so these
data cannot exclude a statistical-learning association of the size they attribute to
working memory. What they establish is that no such association was detected on a
well-measured index, which is why it, and not the neural or inhibitory-control nulls, is the
comparator the specificity argument rests on.

A further scope condition is that no language-specific aptitude test was administered.
All predictors index domain-general capacities, so the contrast our data can draw is
between a single circumscribed capacity and a broad domain-general advantage. It does not
extend to the language-specific aptitude of the Modern Language Aptitude Test (MLAT) and
LLAMA tradition [@li2015]. Whether such an aptitude measure would outpredict working
memory here is an open question.

Finally, the artificial-language design trades ecological validity for control. The gain is
a grammar no participant has met before, so prior exposure cannot confound the
learning curve, and that control is what makes the individual-difference question
tractable at all. The cost is that the three properties enter at different points and
differ in difficulty, so the pooled trajectory averages over learners who are at different
stages of different problems. The pooled analysis is therefore best read alongside the
gender-only one, restricted to the single property sampled from the first grammar session
onwards, which the predictor pattern survived.

## Conclusion

Two lines of evidence point to working memory. It was the one baseline index that predicted
how much grammatical knowledge learners acquired, and the one index that rose across the
training period. Statistical learning, measured at least as reliably, did neither, and the
inhibitory-control measure was too unreliable here to test either way. Both results are
therefore about a single capacity, though the evidence that the pre/post gain is confined
to it stops short of being decisive.

# Data and code availability

All extraction, modelling and reporting scripts, the computational environment
specification and the machine-written summary tables that populate this manuscript are
available in this paper's repository at
<https://github.com/pablobernabeu/LESS-cognitive-predictors>, together with the online
supplementary material. The raw electroencephalographic recordings are too large to
distribute through that repository and are deposited on OSF at <https://osf.io/tq7vy>. The
supplement holds
the baseline predictor distributions and the resting-state spectra, which are descriptive
companions to the analyses reported here and are not needed to interpret them. The
environment specification has two parts, because no single artefact covers the whole of it:
an `renv` lockfile pinning the R packages of the fitting library, snapshotted on the cluster,
and a provenance record written at fit time. The compiler and the optimisation pin described
above belong to neither, being properties of the cluster module, which
is why they are stated in prose. The provenance record covers the software versions in force
when the Part A predictor models were fitted, so those fits can be traced to the environment
that produced them. The pre/post models, the projection-predictive selection and the
cross-validation comparisons run from the same environment, but they write no record of
their own.
`r if (is.null(.prov_tbl) || !nrow(.prov_tbl)) "That record has not yet been written for this paper, which is why the version fields under *Sampler, diagnostics and inference* print as pending. They populate from it automatically once the Part A predictor models are next fitted." else paste0("It was written when those models were fitted, on ", substr(.prov_tbl$recorded_utc[1], 1, 10), ", and it supplies the version fields under *Sampler, diagnostics and inference*.")`

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Convergence diagnostics {#apx-convergence-diagnostics-p2}

Every model whose posterior estimates are reported in the main text was assessed against the same convergence criteria. @tbl-convergence gives the realised per-model values behind the summary in the Results. The common-sample refits behind the cross-validation comparisons are not listed. They exist only to score the two parameterisations on identical observations, carry no reported coefficient and do not pass through the diagnostic artefact.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-convergence
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence Diagnostics for Every Model Whose Posterior Estimates Are Reported"
#| apa-note: "Columns give the maximum rank-normalised split R-hat and the minimum bulk and tail effective sample sizes, each taken over all parameters. Part A models come first, then the Part B pre/post models. The weak-prior rows are the prior-sensitivity refits described under Priors."
if (!is.null(conv_tbl) && requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # Row labels: the CSV carries pipeline identifiers, which are not reader-facing, and it
  # is written in whatever order the summaries job produced. Map to prose names and order
  # rows to follow the manuscript (Part A, then Part B). An identifier with no entry in
  # the map keeps its stripped form rather than being dropped, so a future model still
  # appears.
  .cml <- c(
    predictive_trajectory                     = "Part A: pooled",
    predictive_trajectory_weakprior           = "Part A: pooled (weak priors)",
    predictive_trajectory_gender              = "Part A: gender agreement",
    predictive_trajectory_gender_weakprior    = "Part A: gender agreement (weak priors)",
    predictive_trajectory_gender_iafres       = "Part A: gender agreement, IAF-resolved participants only",
    predictive_trajectory_aperiodic           = "Part A: pooled, aperiodic",
    predictive_trajectory_aperiodic_gender    = "Part A: gender agreement, aperiodic",
    cognition_prepost_digit_span              = "Part B: digit span",
    cognition_prepost_stroop_interference     = "Part B: Stroop interference",
    cognition_prepost_asrt_learning           = "Part B: ASRT learning",
    cognition_prepost_joint                   = "Part B: joint across the three indices",
    cognition_prepost_joint_signaligned       = "Part B: joint across the three indices, sign-aligned")
  conv_tbl <- conv_tbl[order(match(sub("^p2_", "", conv_tbl$model), names(.cml)),
                             conv_tbl$model), , drop = FALSE]
  # Reordering leaves the source row numbers as row names, which kable would print as an
  # unlabelled leading column of pipeline row indices.
  rownames(conv_tbl) <- NULL
  ct <- conv_tbl |>
    dplyr::transmute(Model = ifelse(is.na(.cml[sub("^p2_", "", model)]),
                                    sub("^p2_", "", model),
                                    unname(.cml[sub("^p2_", "", model)])),
                     `max R-hat` = round(max_rhat, 3),
                     `min ESS (bulk)` = round(min_ess_bulk),
                     `min ESS (tail)` = round(min_ess_tail),
                     Divergences = n_divergent,
                     Passed = ifelse(passed, "yes", "no"))
  # Drop a column that carries no information. Every model here has zero divergent
  # transitions and every one passes, so those two columns were a wall of "0" and "yes"
  # restating the sentence above the table, and they were what pushed the header past the
  # measure. They are dropped only when they are genuinely constant, so a future run in
  # which a model diverges or fails still shows it rather than hiding it.
  if (all(!is.na(ct$Divergences)) && all(ct$Divergences == 0)) ct$Divergences <- NULL
  if (all(ct$Passed == "yes"))                ct$Passed      <- NULL
  knitr::kable(ct)
} else {
  cat("*Convergence diagnostics will appear here once the models are fitted.*")
}
```

# Reliability of the baseline predictors {#apx-predictor-reliability}

@tbl-predictor-reliability gives the split-half internal consistency of the three baseline cognitive indices. The values, and what they imply for the inhibitory-control null, are discussed under *Limitations and future directions*.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictor-reliability
#| tbl-cap: "Internal-Consistency Reliability of the Three Baseline Cognitive Predictors at Session 1"
#| apa-note: "Reliability is estimated by permutation split-half: each participant's trials are repeatedly split in half, the index is recomputed on each half, the halves are correlated across participants, and the mean correlation is corrected to full test length by the Spearman-Brown formula. Two of the three indices (Stroop interference, ASRT learning) are difference scores."
if (!is.null(predrel_tbl) && requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  .prl <- c(digit_span = "Working memory (digit span)",
            stroop_interference = "Inhibitory control (Stroop interference)",
            asrt_learning = "Statistical learning (ASRT)")
  # Correlations and reliabilities are bounded by 1, so their leading zeros are stripped,
  # matching predrel() and relv() in the running prose.
  .strip0 <- function(x) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))
  pr <- predrel_tbl |>
    dplyr::transmute(Predictor = unname(.prl[predictor]),
                     `Participants` = n_participants,
                     `Mean half-test r` = .strip0(r_half),
                     `Reliability (Spearman-Brown)` = .strip0(reliability_sb),
                     `Random splits` = n_splits)
  knitr::kable(pr)
} else {
  cat("*Predictor reliability will appear once `scripts/11_extract_predictor_reliability.R` has run.*")
}
```

# Supplementary materials {#apx-supplementary}

The two displays below are supplied to the journal as online supplementary material
and are deposited with the analysis code in this paper's repository. They are
descriptive companions to the intercorrelations and numerical summaries in the main
text, so they are not required to interpret the findings, and they fall outside the
five figures of the article proper. @fig-predictor-dist shows the distribution of each
baseline predictor over the stored records for that measure, and @fig-rs-psd the
resting-state spectra behind the band-power and individual-alpha-frequency predictors.

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictor-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of the Baseline Predictors"
#| apa-note: "Violins with individual points show working memory (digit span), Stroop interference and ASRT statistical-learning scores, and the eyes-closed resting-state band powers and individual alpha frequency. Each panel is drawn from the stored records for that measure, so the number of points differs between panels and exceeds the model samples reported under Participants. Difference-score predictors (Stroop, ASRT) are shown on their raw scale, and each panel's unit is given in its label. Box plots mark the median and interquartile range. The absolute band powers are strongly right-skewed. They nonetheless enter the models z-scored on this raw scale, with no transform applied. Points at the 7 Hz floor of the individual-alpha-frequency panel are values at the lower bound of the estimator's search range, not necessarily measured peaks (see Cognitive and neural indices)."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
pred_vals <- .read_csv_if(paper2_results("_predictor_values.csv"))
if (!is.null(pred_vals)) {
  ord <- c("digit_span", "stroop_interference", "asrt_learning",
           "delta", "theta", "alpha", "beta", "gamma", "iaf")
  pred_vals$predictor <- factor(pred_vals$predictor, levels = ord)
  # Units differ across predictors and the y scales are free, so each panel states its
  # own unit: the cognitive indices are a count and two reaction-time differences, the
  # band powers a power integrated over frequency, and the individual alpha frequency a
  # frequency. The band unit is uV^2, NOT uV^2/Hz: 03_extract_resting_state_eeg.R defines
  # band power as the trapezoidal integral of the PSD over the band, which cancels the
  # per-Hz denominator. fig-rs-psd, which plots the density itself, keeps uV^2/Hz.
  pred_lab <- as_labeller(c(
    digit_span = "Digit span (items correct)", stroop_interference = "Stroop (ms)",
    asrt_learning = "ASRT (ms)", delta = "Delta (µV²)",
    theta = "Theta (µV²)", alpha = "Alpha (µV²)",
    beta = "Beta (µV²)", gamma = "Gamma (µV²)",
    iaf = "IAF (Hz)"))
  ggplot(pred_vals, aes(x = "", y = value)) +
    geom_violin(fill = "grey90", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.12, size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey25") +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.10, fill = "white", colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3, outlier.shape = NA) +
    facet_wrap(~ predictor, scales = "free_y", nrow = 3, labeller = pred_lab) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + les_theme() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
} else cat("*Predictor distributions will appear once `_predictor_values.csv` is present.*")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rs-psd
#| fig-cap: "Grand-Average Resting-State Power Spectral Density Over the Eight Occipito-Parietal Electrodes"
#| apa-note: "Eyes-closed is shown against eyes-open. Both axes are logarithmic, so the aperiodic 1/f background appears as a straight line. The curve is the geometric mean across every recorded resting-state spectrum, a wider frame than the fitted models use, and the shaded ribbon is the interquartile range. Grey lines mark the interior delta/theta/alpha/beta/gamma band edges (4, 8, 13, 30 Hz), and the alpha band (8--13 Hz) is highlighted. The darker region above 30 Hz lies beyond the offline low-pass corner: the nominal gamma band (30--45 Hz) falls entirely within it, which is why that predictor is not interpreted. The eyes-closed posterior alpha increase (alpha-blocking on eye opening) is the expected Berger effect, which serves here as a check on the recording and the reduction."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
if (!is.null(psd_tbl)) {
  ga <- psd_tbl |>
    dplyr::group_by(condition, freq_hz) |>
    dplyr::summarise(lo = stats::quantile(power, .25, na.rm = TRUE),
                     hi = stats::quantile(power, .75, na.rm = TRUE),
                     power = exp(mean(log(power), na.rm = TRUE)),
                     .groups = "drop")
  cond_lab <- c(eyes_closed = "Eyes closed", eyes_open = "Eyes open")
  ggplot(ga, aes(freq_hz, power, colour = condition)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 8, xmax = 13, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08, fill = "grey40") +
    # Shade the region above the 30 Hz offline low-pass corner. The nominal gamma band
    # (30-45 Hz) lies entirely inside it, so the figure shows directly why that predictor
    # is not interpretable rather than leaving the point to the text.
    annotate("rect", xmin = 30, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.13, fill = "grey55") +
    annotate("text", x = 37, y = Inf, label = "above low-pass", vjust = 1.6,
             size = 2.8, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 8, 13, 30), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = condition), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
    geom_line(aes(linetype = condition), linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 13, 20, 30, 45), labels = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 13, 20, 30, 45)) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(eyes_closed = "#D55E00", eyes_open = "#0072B2"), labels = cond_lab) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(eyes_closed = "#D55E00", eyes_open = "#0072B2"), guide = "none") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(eyes_closed = "solid", eyes_open = "22"), labels = cond_lab) +
    labs(x = "Frequency (Hz)", y = expression(Power~(mu*V^2/Hz)), colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
    les_theme() + theme(legend.position = "top")
} else cat("*Resting-state spectra will appear once `_resting_state_psd.csv` is present.*")
```
